prompt: The writer argues chiefly that
passage:
Pye and Son of Marram print 1691 on their wrappers, on the fascia over the shop, and on the fourth page of the town's visitor brochure, where the business is called the oldest bakery in England still working from one address. I have spent two winters on that claim. I can say what it rests on, and I can say what it is worth.

It rests on two things, and both of them are real. A date-stone cut with the year 1691 is set in the wall of the yard behind the shop, four feet above the ground and directly over the oven's stoke-hole. And a deed of 1742 conveys the bakehouse in Fore Street to one Josiah Pye, who is certainly an ancestor of the family that bakes there now.

The stone was not cut for that wall. Marram's Independent chapel was pulled down in 1889, and the builder who took the contract, Henry Flack, kept a day-book which is in the county office and which anybody may call up. Under 4 September he entered the carriage of the datestone and two corbels from the chapel yard to Fore Street, and charged three shillings for setting the first of them. The chapel was built in 1691. The stone has been telling the truth about the chapel for three hundred years, and telling it, since 1889, on the wrong wall.

The deed is honest too, and it is about a different building. Fore Street was renumbered in 1866, when the four cottages at the top were taken down and the street was counted from the church end instead of the bridge end. The bakehouse conveyed in 1742 stood at what is now number 31, which is the chemist's; the deed's own boundaries name the smithy on one side and the churchyard wall on the other, and neither of those has ever touched the present shop, which stands sixty yards off and on the opposite side.

What is true is better than what is printed, and it is out in the yard. The oven is brick-lined, and the bricks are the long thin sort made before the tax on brick sizes changed the trade's habits after 1803. The firm's own coal accounts begin in 1799, and they open with a repair to the oven, not with its building. Nobody else in this county has a working oven that can be shown to be as old. That is a distinction, it is defensible, and it is the claim they ought to be making.

I have no quarrel with the Pyes. The family did not invent the date; a brochure writer handed it to them in 1974 and they have been living up to it ever since, and I do not think it is a baker's business to audit a brochure. The wrapper is another matter. It is printed by the thousand, it is wrong, and it is the only thing about that shop most people will ever read. Drop the line, put the oven in its place, and they lose nothing but a sentence.

the oven behind the shop ought to be protected before it is repaired again

the bakery's own papers were dispersed in 1889, and its true age can no longer be settled

The pearl mussel of the Bann Beck lives in one reach and has never been recorded anywhere else in the catchment: two kilometres of gravel between the Ing Bridge and the sheep creep at Waddow. Above the bridge the beck runs over rock and holds none. Below the creep the bed is peat, and none has ever been found there.

In 1985 the Fell Ing Angling Association walked the reach in waders with glass-bottomed buckets and counted four thousand one hundred shells. In 2019 the same stretch was walked the same way by two of the same people, and the count was sixty.

Two things happened to the beck in 1997, and they happened within five weeks of each other. Ellerby Farm, half a mile above the Ing Bridge, replaced an open midden with a covered store and moved its spreading from October to February. And the drainage board dredged the beck from the bridge down to the creep, lifting out the gravel bars and squaring the channel.

The farm's run-off enters above the bridge and passes down the whole reach; the dredger worked from the bridge to the creep and stopped there; and those two kilometres are the entire range of the animal. Edith Marr converted about two hundred turret clocks to electric winding between 1961 and 1989, and refused perhaps thirty more. It is the refusals her trade remembers her for, and the rule behind them is written inside the front cover of every one of her job-books, in eleven words: convert where the fall is gone, not where the winder is tired.

A turret clock is driven by weights on ropes that fall the height of the tower, and the weight of a clock is calculated against the distance it has to drop. When a tower is shortened, or a ringing floor is put in below the clock chamber, or a stair is boxed in across the weight shaft, that fall is cut, and a clock that was built to run eight days on one winding will not run three. Those Marr converted without argument, and most of her two hundred were of that kind. What she would not do was put a motor on a sound clock because the winding had become a nuisance to a parish.

Nether Hallam wrote to her in the spring of 1974. Their winder of thirty-one years had died in the February and they had found nobody to take it on, and they asked what a conversion would cost. The white is not the worse paper; it is much the better one, hot-pressed and evenly made, and it cost the firm three times as much. But it came from a mill that sized its sheets while a chloride from the bleaching was still in them, and the blue is a lake struck on an alumina base, which gives up its colour to a chloride slowly and completely over thirty or forty years. The straw-board was never bleached at all.
